angle: This deck looks like group hug and is actually a court: every engine hands the whole table cards, and the cards are the sentence — you run the docket patiently as a draw-go control deck (the honest number says two games in three), then pass sentence only inside the verified windows.

departments.note: Heliod at hero scale from the pilot's actual March of the Machine printing, collector number 17, art by Victor Adame Minguez — credit line under the art, per the featured-artist convention. The tagline 'Everyone draws. Everyone pays.' is the issue's angle in four words; let it sit directly under the deck name. The dominant coverline sells the issue's crown jewel: the same pair of cards the combo database calls infinite was refuted by the checker (A-001), and the three-card version was then verified (A-004) — both halves are checker-passed fact, so the cover can promise both without inflation. Do not add a third violator, and do not tease the Aetherflux kill: it is unverified and the cover may not promise it.

Two-bucket contents plus the tier legend printed in full — Vol. 004, but every issue is somebody's first. In the THIS ISSUE'S DECK bucket, the one-line promise for The Kill should read 'three verified lines and one famous fake' so the refutation is promised from page two.

departments.headline: THE GENEROSITY TRAP
departments.dek: Why would a control deck hand every opponent an extra card, every turn, on purpose? Because in this deck the cards aren't a gift — they're evidence, and the sentence is read at each opponent's upkeep.

callouts.title: LOOK LIKE A GIFT
callouts.text: Turns one through three are Remora into rock into Kami — the curve the deck was built to play. Howling Mine effects read as group hug, and you should let them: eighteen lands plus nine rocks keep you on schedule while the table files you under harmless.

callouts.title: LAND THE HINGE
callouts.text: Heliod arrives on turn 4 in the majority of simulated games — 5,155 of 10,000 on turn 4 exactly, 90.5% by turn 6. The front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the {3}{U/P} flip is the moment the deck turns on, and it can only ever happen at sorcery speed.

callouts.title: OPEN THE COURT
callouts.text: The Warped Eclipse grants everything flash and discounts your spells {1} for each card your opponents drew this turn. Your own Mines pay your mana bill: on a Font of Mythos board, one table rotation can make your next spell nearly free — cast at instant speed, counterspells still up.

callouts.title: PASS SENTENCE
callouts.text: The punishers convert hand size into upkeep damage: once Forced Fruition has filled a hand, cleanup trims it to exactly seven and the next upkeep costs them 7 — verified, and it repeats every rotation without you tapping a land. When the court can't convene, Approach of the Second Sun is the clean exit.

captions.Howling Mine: **THE BAIT:** an extra card for everyone at each draw step. Perfectly symmetric on its face — the punishers and Heliod's discount are what make it yours.
captions.Forced Fruition: **THE DETONATOR:** every opponent spell becomes seven forced draws. Nobody stays under the punisher threshold once this resolves.

pilot_tips.text: Check your opener for Leyline of Anticipation — it comes down free before turn one and makes every engine piece a flash play, which is Heliod's back face a full three turns early.

departments.pull_quote: The cards aren't a gift. They're evidence.

departments.headline: THEIR DRAWS, YOUR DISCOUNT
departments.dek: Your commander is the one card you are guaranteed to have — so what is that worth when the card is a hinge the whole deck turns on? Here, it is the single most reliable event in 10,000 simulations, and the tax math has a wrinkle no other deck in this series has had.
departments.body: Start with the guarantee. The command zone means Heliod is not a card you hope to draw: he is face up before the first mulligan is offered, and the simulator confirms what guaranteed access is worth — mean cast turn 4.125, median 4, down by turn 6 in 90.5% of games, the most dependable number in the whole issue. That is why Keep or Ship never asks your opening hand for a commander, an engine payoff or a win condition: the deck's hinge is already on the table, and your seven cards only need to buy the turns before him. The tax ladder reads 4, then 6, then 8, then 10 — but this commander's real recast cost is the wrinkle: Heliod always returns front-face-up, so every recast is tax PLUS another {3}{U/P} PLUS another sorcery-speed window you may never safely get. That math is why protection beats recasting here more decisively than usual — the commander-insurance spend is Lightning Greaves through the flip window and a counterspell held for the removal, because you are not protecting a 4/4, you are protecting a transform activation you cannot take reactively. Color identity is its own lesson: the front face is mono-white, but a double-faced card's identity is the union of its faces, and the blue back face is the entire reason this is a WU deck — without the Warped Eclipse, two-thirds of the 99 would be illegal. The 21-damage clock, for once, is a coincidence: a 4/4 needs six connections and this deck plans zero of them. And the political read: the Radiant Dawn resolving looks like a pillow-fort enchantment deck, and the table will treat it that way — but a turn-one Rhystic Study or Mystic Remora tells every experienced pilot what bracket you actually are, because this list's floor is 4 on the strength of eight Game Changers alone. The zone guarantees the hinge; the format guarantees the tell.

captions.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: **THE HINGE:** the front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the {3}{U/P} flip — sorcery speed only, 2 life if you're short a blue — makes your whole deck flash and bills your spells to the table's draw count.
captions.Lightning Greaves: **THE INSURANCE:** shroud through the flip window costs two mana. An answered Heliod costs tax, another {3}{U/P}, and a sorcery window you may never get back.

pilot_tips.text: Equip the Greaves the turn you plan to flip, not the turn Heliod lands — the transform is the one action this deck can never take reactively, so it is the thing worth insuring.

departments.pull_quote: You are not protecting a 4/4. You are protecting a sorcery-speed activation you only get to take while he lives.

departments.headline: TEN THOUSAND QUIET GAMES
departments.dek: We ran the list 10,000 times on seed 42, and the deck's two best numbers belong to its commander and its counterspells — not its engine. One number on this page is here specifically to keep you honest.

callouts.title: 73.6% KEEPABLE
callouts.text: 73.6% of first sevens are keeps at 0.336 mulligans per game. Eighteen lands sounds reckless until you see the kept-hand distribution centered on 2–3 lands plus rocks — the nine mana rocks are load-bearing, not filler.

callouts.title: TURN 4, LIKE CLOCKWORK
callouts.text: The commander histogram spikes at turn 4 — 5,155 of 10,000 games — with mean 4.125 and 90.5% by turn 6. Heliod is the most reliable event in the deck; the plan can afford patience everywhere else because the hinge shows up on a date.

callouts.title: THE HONEST NUMBER: 34.3%
callouts.text: 'Engine + punisher assembled', the deck's core two-piece, lands by turn 6 in 34.3% of games — 49.1% ever. Read that plainly: in most games you are not the punisher deck. You are a draw-go control deck waiting for the court to convene.

callouts.title: SAYING NO IN 73.4%
callouts.text: Free or cheap interaction is in hand by turn 6 in 61.9% of games and 73.4% overall — nearly identical to the keep rate. Holding up an answer is not a fallback plan; it is the statistically dominant line.

captions.Thought Vessel: **LAB NOTE:** rocks contribute from the turn after they land in this model — and mean available mana still hits 4.24 on turn 4 and 4.96 on turn 5. Heliod on four, the flip on five: the schedule pays for itself.

pilot_tips.text: Lead Ancient Tomb into a two-mana rock whenever the opener offers it — that line is how 27.7% of simulated games put Heliod down by turn 3.

departments.pull_quote: In two games out of three, you are not the punisher deck yet. Play like it.
departments.note: The stated-assumptions box is non-negotiable and this issue it earns its keep twice: the model simulates resource development, not games — and it does not model cost reducers, which means every number on this page ignores Heliod's discount entirely. The real deck is faster than the chart; the chart is the floor. Say exactly that, in the lab voice, no rounding.

departments.headline: COURT IS IN SESSION
departments.dek: Four lines went to the adversarial checker and all four came back stamped. Two win the game, one is an engine that wins nothing on its own — and one is a famous infinite this deck does not have, which is precisely why you can believe the other three.

callouts.title: THE TRIGGER SITS ON TOP
callouts.text: The default win, under fire: an opponent aims Naturalize at Forced Fruition, and the Fruition trigger goes on the stack above the very spell that caused it. They draw their seven cards before the enchantment dies — the ability resolves no matter what happens to its source. FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-003.

callouts.title: CLEANUP DOES YOUR HOMEWORK
callouts.text: At the end of their turn, the cleanup step trims that inflated hand back to exactly seven cards — which happens to be precisely the threshold both punishers want. You did not spend a card or a mana on this part.

callouts.title: SEVEN AT THE BELL
callouts.text: Next upkeep: Ebony Owl Netsuke sees seven-plus cards and deals 4; Iron Maiden deals hand-size-minus-four for 3. Seven damage, from you, with every land untapped — and because cleanup reloads the hand to seven each rotation, the clock re-arms itself.

callouts.title: BURY THE SUN, DIG IT UP
callouts.text: The clean exit: Approach of the Second Sun's first cast gains 7 life and buries it seventh from the top — trivially shallow when everyone is drawing in bulk. Mystical Tutor at an end step puts it back on top on demand. FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-002.

callouts.title: THE ONLY WINDOW
callouts.text: The second cast wins during resolution, as a spell effect — and the first casting still counts even though the card was shuffled away, because the game tracks the event, not the card. The table's one and only window is while the second Approach is on the stack; the case file plays out the counter-war, Swan Song included.

callouts.title: AN ENGINE, NOT A KILL
callouts.text: Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring + Arcane Signet is a verified unbounded-cast loop: each rock's cast bounces the other, tapping each before it leaves keeps the cycle at exactly 3 mana in, 3 out. It nets no mana, no cards, no damage. The Aetherflux Reservoir exit is a candidate that still needs a stack scenario — we will not call it a kill until the checker does. And the two-card version the database believes in? Refuted. FULL DOSSIER: A-001 and A-004.

captions.Forced Fruition: **THE VERDICT DELIVERED:** seven forced draws per opponent spell — and the trigger resolves even when the spell that fired it is the removal that kills it.
captions.Ebony Owl Netsuke: **EXHIBIT A:** a flat 4 at each opponent's upkeep at seven-plus cards. Two mana, bought in 1996 money, dealing 2026 damage.
captions.Iron Maiden: **EXHIBIT B:** hand size minus four, computed on resolution — which means cards added in response to the trigger count against them.
captions.Approach of the Second Sun: **THE CLEAN EXIT:** the win is checked mid-resolution, not by state-based action. Once every player passes on the second cast, nothing in the game can stop it.
captions.Hullbreaker Horror: **THE ENGINE, AUDITED:** with Sol Ring alone, nothing — the trigger can't target your own spell on the stack. With Sol Ring plus a true two-mana rock, unbounded casts in one main phase.

pilot_tips.text: Hold Swan Song for the counter-war on the second Approach — a 2/2 Bird is a bargain against winning the game, and the case file shows exactly where it slots into the stack.
Aim Stroke of Genius at the punished player while Iron Maiden's trigger is on the stack — the Maiden counts their hand on resolution, so every card you force is another point of damage.

departments.pull_quote: The clock runs during everyone else's draw step. Once it's live, your only job is protecting it.
departments.note: One feature spread per verified line, in this order: A-003 (the default win) gets the marquee scenario-box, A-002 second, A-004 third with the refutation callout attached. Citations stay in Judge's Desk; this department narrates. The Aetherflux exit is flagged 'needs a stack scenario' wherever it is mentioned — no exceptions.

departments.headline: GUILTY OF LOOKING HARMLESS
departments.dek: The table will misread you twice — first as group hug, then as a combo deck you factually are not. Both misreads are assets, but only if you manage them on purpose.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: Engine plus punisher on the battlefield with Heliod flipped: that is the board state that makes you archenemy, and once it exists you should embrace it openly — the verified clock deals 7 on each punished upkeep and re-arms every rotation without you tapping out. Before that board exists, you are a draw-go deck whose Mines read as generosity. Let them.

callouts.title: THE LOUDEST TELL
callouts.text: Mystical Tutor at your last opponent's end step with seven-plus mana implied is this deck's one unmistakable signal — every pilot who has seen an Approach deck knows exactly what goes on top. Count the table's open blue before you fire it, hold Dovin's Veto or Swan Song for the commit turn, and never telegraph it a rotation early.

callouts.title: THE FALSE ALARM
callouts.text: Some tables will 'know' you as the Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring infinite deck — 296,000 database decks say so. Case A-001 says otherwise: with only those two cards, no repeatable sequence exists. You can correct the misread to buy peace, or let removal chase a threat you don't actually have. Either is fine; choosing by accident is not.

captions.Rhystic Study: **THE BRACKET TELL:** turn-one Rhystic Study tells every experienced pilot what the hug costume is hiding — this list floors at bracket 4 on eight Game Changers.
captions.Mystic Remora: **THE EARLY READ:** a turn-one Remora looks like value. Against a spell-dense pod it is a firehose, and the table's veterans know it.

pilot_tips.text: Spend Teferi's Protection on the Farewell-class sweeper, not the alpha strike — it phases out your entire punisher board, which is the asset the attack was never going to touch.
Fetch Homeward Path the moment a theft deck sits down — everyone takes their own creatures back, and at this table 'everyone' usually means you.

departments.pull_quote: Let them file you under group hug. You're not a hug. You're a court.

departments.headline: TWO TABLES, NO TAKEBACKS
departments.dek: One turn asks whether generosity is safe with a spellslinger across the table; the other asks when a god should change faces. Read each board, commit out loud, and only then read the bench's ruling.

callouts.title: HOW TO PLAY ALONG
callouts.text: Cover the recommendation box with your hand. Read the board, pick a branch, say it out loud — the signals and coalition risks are printed with each branch precisely so you can argue with them. Being wrong on this page is free; being wrong at the table costs a game.

pilot_tips.text: Deploy Dictate of Kruphix at the end of the turn before the upkeep you most want taxed — flash means the extra draws start exactly where you point them.
Use Folio of Fancies' X-activation as a precision tool: push exactly the hand you want over seven, exactly when the punishers are about to ask.

departments.pull_quote: The flip is the one action this deck can never take reactively. Its risk compounds every cycle it waits.
departments.note: Two spreads from the decision artifacts: 001 (turn 6 — does Forced Fruition come down against a spellslinger?) and 002 (turn 7 — when does Heliod become the Warped Eclipse?). The recommendation must sit visually below the branches in both; neither dek nor headline may hint at the answers.

departments.headline: WHO BREAKS THE COURT
departments.dek: Creature wraths hit almost nothing you care about, and one archetype turns your own engine into their best card. Can you name the pod where the correct play is holding Forced Fruition all game?

threats.read: This is the one. Your draw engines, all three punishers, nine mana rocks, Propaganda and Ghostly Prison sit in a single blast radius, while creature wraths hit a handful of utility bodies you can rebuild. Deploy the engine in layers instead of dumping it, bank countermagic for the one spell that takes the board, and remember Heliod's front face rebuys an enchantment on every recast — the court can reconvene if you kept the pieces staggered.
outs: Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the Warped Eclipse

threats.read: Be honest with yourself: your engine is their engine, and Forced Fruition hands a storm pilot seven cards per spell. Against these pods, holding it is a real line, not cowardice. Deploy the asymmetric layer instead — a turn-one Remora against a spell-dense pod is one of the best cards in your 99 — and spend the free suite by the answer-economy bar: counter the ritual engine or the payoff, never the cantrip.

Every deck that wins 'on resolution' has one interaction window exactly like your Approach does, and your job is knowing theirs as precisely as you know yours. Free counter on the enabler, Swords on the reanimated body, overloaded Rift when the window has already passed. The judgment flag: your forced draws fill delve and escape graveyards as a side effect — against those decks the Mine effects cost more than they look.

You are the control deck and happy about it. One pillow-fort enchantment taxes three players' attack steps — virtual card advantage tripled — and the punishers push an aggro deck's damage-per-card below what 40 life demands. The trap is sequencing: Forced Fruition into an empty aggro hand is a full refill of live threats, so land punishers before or with the big draw pieces, and save the exile removal for the one commander that ignores fort taxes.

pilot_tips.text: Against storm and spellslinger pods, hold Forced Fruition all game if you must — seven free cards per spell is a donation those decks convert faster than your punishers can tax it.
The basic land you gift with Path is a real cost at a taxed table — save it for the creature that actually kills you, not the first one that attacks.

departments.pull_quote: Your engine is their engine. Whether that's a weapon or a liability is decided by who's sitting across from you.

departments.headline: ENGINES, PUNISHERS, AND THE LAW
departments.dek: Eighty-five cards doing five jobs: feed the table, tax the hand, keep your own draws asymmetric, say no, or end it. The load-bearing cards lead — and the role histogram famously can't see half of them.

roster.role: The court: engines that feed the table

captions.Consecrated Sphinx: **THE MAGNET:** two cards to you per card an opponent draws — fourteen per opponent spell under Forced Fruition, and the strongest removal magnet you play.
captions.Temple Bell: **THE INSTANT-SPEED HUG:** a draw for everyone, on demand — ring it in response to removal for pure value, or to push a hand where the punishers want it.

departments.note: Rank matters: the punisher core and the engines lead, mana closes. Say the honest structural fact out loud in the intro — 24 of these cards, including nearly the entire punisher core, have no entry in the role taxonomy, so anyone judging this list by a role histogram will conclude it has no plan. The histogram is wrong; the plan is on this page. Tiles are role-first and carry no printing credits — the physical cards belong to Featured Artist.

departments.headline: SEVENTY-FOUR HANDS
departments.dek: Nobody painted more than three cards in this deck — 74 artists across 85 entries, the flattest credits page in this series so far. So who leads a deck with no favorites, and what does a list like that tell you about how it was built?

featured.note: John Avon leads this deck's credits with exactly three cards: Fellwar Stone, Mikokoro, Center of the Sea, and the Plains art — and that lead is the story, because three is the most anyone painted here. Count per copy and you'd crown a different artist entirely: Ron Spears' Island appears eleven times and Avon's Plains six, which is why this department counts per card, always — repetition is printing, not authorship. There is no Secret Lair run hiding in these numbers, no collector-number streak, no product bought whole: seventy-four artists across eighty-five entries is what a deck looks like when it is assembled one card at a time across three decades of sets, from Mark Tedin's Braingeyser to this year's printings. And if one Avon card earns the hero slot, it is Mikokoro, Center of the Sea — the whole issue's thesis painted onto a land: everyone gets a card, it can't be countered, and it survives every board wipe in the format.

also_worth_noting.note: Two cards, one lineage: Braingeyser and Temple Bell — the game's oldest everyone-draws job and its bell-shaped descendant, decades apart, same hand.
Both of the deck's flash haymakers are his: Hullbreaker Horror and Torrential Gearhulk, the two creatures that arrive mid-counter-war.
Sol Ring and White Sun's Zenith — the engine's cheapest piece and the library-dwelling finisher, two cards that never want to be in the same turn.

captions.Mikokoro, Center of the Sea: **THE THESIS, PAINTED:** John Avon's island hands every player a card — uncounterable, wrath-proof, and exactly what this deck is for.
captions.Braingeyser: **THE ELDER:** Mark Tedin's Braingeyser is the oldest job in the deck — force-feeding a hand past seven has been blue's business since the beginning.

departments.pull_quote: Repetition is printing, not authorship. We count the cards, not the copies.
departments.note: The analysis reports no standout (lead artist: 3 entries) and no drop runs — this is the breadth story the spec promises for exactly this case. Art File fast-facts from the computed credits: 85 entries, 100 copies, 74 artists, 0 foils, 0 borderless, top set Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander at 7 entries by 7 different artists.

departments.headline: FOUR OPENERS, FOUR RULINGS
departments.dek: The sim keeps 73.6% of first sevens, so the question is rarely whether to keep — it's which of these four you would ship anyway. Rule on each before you read the bench's reason.

hands.why: Three lands, a rock, an asymmetric engine, a table engine, and something that says no — the exact bar: two to four lands, one card-flow piece, an answer. Heliod needs no help from your seven; he arrives by turn 6 in 90.5% of games on his own.

Ancient Tomb into a two-mana rock is the deck's accelerant — the line behind the 27.7% of games that land Heliod by turn 3. Kami is the cheapest engine in the 99, Rhystic is the bracket tell you cash on turn one, and two interaction pieces cover the gap.

hands.verdict: SHIP — a courtroom with no plaintiffs
hands.why: Three punishers and not one card that makes anybody draw. Iron Maiden against a normal five-card hand is one damage a turn — the punishers are inert until the engine exists, and this hand is a mulligan in costume. Two lands, no rock, no flow. Ship it.

Three lands and four cards that are all the back half of a game. Nothing here draws, taxes, or says no — and you never mulligan chasing Approach anyway: win-condition access shows up in 61% of games on its own, and the tutors find it when the board is ready.

captions.Mystic Remora: **THE UPGRADE:** the card that turns a marginal keep into a live one — a turn-one Remora often banks three-plus cards before the upkeep bites.

pilot_tips.text: Pay Remora's cumulative upkeep two or three times, then let it go — the ages are a fee, not a mortgage, and the cards are already banked.

departments.pull_quote: You are mulliganing toward flow plus interaction — never toward the lock.

departments.headline: NOTHING OBSOLETES AN IRON MAIDEN
departments.dek: The obsolescence index has real opinions about this mana base and no idea what a punisher is for. What it got right, what it got narrow — and a negative result that is the best news in the issue.

pilot_tips.text: Make Worn Powerstone your first cut when trimming — it enters tapped, costs three, and the verified loop math already excludes it: the engine needs a castable two-drop that taps the turn it lands.
Ignore the index's Sol Ring comparison here — Fellwar's real demerit is the verified one: it sustains the Hullbreaker loop only while an opponent's land can actually produce mana.

The index says Mystical Tutor obsoletes it, but the supersession is narrower than it looks — Plans fetches permanents: a punisher, the Reservoir, the missing loop rock. Keep both until a slot is on fire.
The index offers Syncopate and Spell Snare on cost. Both are conditional by their own text — a poor trade in a deck that plans to hold mana anyway. Note it and move on.

departments.pull_quote: Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, Viseling, Howling Mine, Font of Mythos: zero obsolescence entries. Nothing printed since does this job better — the old cards are the tech, not the debt.
departments.note: The index is format-agnostic and cannot see this deck's pillars; every suggestion above is audited against them, and the audit is the department. Azorius Signet's Mind Stone entry and Brass Infiniscope's Daily Bugle Newspaper entry can run as one-line fast-facts with the honest caveats: colored fixing versus late-game cash-in, and whether the X-spell rider ever fires.

departments.headline: FOUR FILES, ONE OVERTURNED PRECEDENT
departments.dek: Eighty-six verbatim citations across four case files. A-001 overturns a two-card 'infinite' that 296,000 database decks believe in; A-004 establishes the three-card engine that actually works — the same cards, the same rules, opposite verdicts, both stamped.
departments.note: Renderer-generated from the checker-passed artifacts; nothing summarized, truncated, or paraphrased. Case order A-001 through A-004, with A-001 and A-004 presented as a linked pair — the refute-then-verify arc is the evidence contract performing in public and deserves a connecting file tab. Case status lines: A-003 and A-004 each passed on the second iteration; say so — the checker sending work back is the reason the stamp means anything.

Next issue is TO BE ANNOUNCED per issue.json — run the teaser as authored, do not invent a deck. Colophon carries the rules version from the stack artifacts, the decklist sha256 (1813c487…), seed 42, and the Fan Content Policy line. Close the loop on the angle in one line above the colophon: court adjourned.

rhythm_notes: The canonical order already alternates cleanly this issue: By the Numbers (dense analysis) hands off to The Kill, whose six callout-steps read as narrative — the built-in breather doing its job. The Kill is the peak and gets the most ambitious layout: three feature spreads plus the refutation callout. Politics (reflection) recovers from it, What's Your Play re-engages, and Know Your Enemy's four threat-boxes (reference) are followed by two deliberately low-intensity browsing pages — The 99 and the breadth-story Featured Artist, whose pull quote is the issue's quietest page and is placed there on purpose. Keep or Ship re-activates the reader before the light Upgrade Watch, and Judge's Desk stays opt-in manila at the back. The 001-refutation is told at three depths — a cover violator, a Kill callout, and the full A-001 dossier — each one a level deeper, never merely repeated.
gaps: The Aetherflux Reservoir lethal off the verified 004 engine is the highest-value stack to resolve next — it would upgrade The Kill's 'an engine, not a kill' spread into a third verified win. Until then it is flagged 'needs a stack scenario' in every mention.
Three more candidate lines remain unverified and are only teased as candidates: Psychosis Crawler + mass X-draw, Smothering Tithe's treasure yield under Forced Fruition, and Displacer Kitten chains.

Strategy DB holes the frame already names: no school for the hug/slug donation-risk calculus, none for hand-size as an attack vector, none for forced-draw feeding mill — Politics and Know Your Enemy coach from adjacent schools (threat-deflection, critical-mass, answer-economy) and say so.
